title: A Piece of Pi: Embedding The OpenClaw Coding Agent In Your Product — Matthias Luebken, Tavon

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on agent structure: LLM-tool loops, harnesses (Agent MDE), sessions, hooks, events, and multi-channel plugin mechanisms for orchestrating sub-agents. Pi is a developer SDK for building agents, and the primary application is a B2B sales pipeline embedded in enterprise operations. The talk covers building agents with Pi's SDK and deploying them in a production sales pipeline with customer-specific sessions. Requires familiarity with TypeScript, LLMs, and tool calling, but does not assume deep ML or infrastructure expertise. This is a conference talk from the AI Engineer channel presented by Matthias Luebken. All evidence anchors are directly said in the transcript with grade 'said_in_transcript'.

summary: Matthias Luebken explores embedding Pi—a minimal, open-source coding agent SDK—in real products, using OpenClaw as the entry point. He frames the field as nascent: no authoritative patterns exist for coding agents yet, and everything shown may change within weeks. His guiding philosophy comes from Ken Thompson's Unix principle of writing programs that do one thing well, which he argues aligns naturally with agents. He cites Cohere/Claude's desktop as an example: rather than directly integrating Excel, it bundles small CLI tools (Pandas, OpenPyXL, LibreOffice) into a skill, making the agent's job easier. The central architectural pattern is to make systems easy for coding agents—think about what agents are good at and design data access and tool interfaces accordingly. An agent is defined simply as an LLM running tools in a loop: given goals and context, it calls tools, receives results, and repeats. Pi's core agent is TypeScript-based with an agent class, event system, and hooks for pre-tool-call logic. He demonstrates a CRM lead qualifier with a terminal interface using about three TypeScript files. Coding agents extend this model by adding a runtime and shell (Bash). The extension API enables session events and UI interactions including context UI select. OpenClaw builds on Pi's core packages (coding agent, agent core, Pi AI for unified LLM abstraction, terminal UI) and adds its own plugin mechanism for multi-channel routing, provider orchestration, sub-agents, and gateway support. The main application example is a B2B sales pipeline for a client: incoming RFP emails are monitored and routed through a gateway to customer-specific agent sessions. Each agent has a general harness (Agent MDE) defining its role and a customer-specific file (Customer MD) describing quirks, discounts, and access rules. Sessions are created and reused per case for context continuity. CRM and ERP data is exposed via CLIs because agents are good at using CLIs, with sandboxing for security. The only human-facing output is a draft email in the user's inbox—users stay in their email client and edit drafts freely, while multiple agents work under the hood performing tool calls in loops. Luebken notes they are exploring Nvidia's open shell announcement for sandboxing. He concludes with takeaways: coding agents are and will be a core building block for software systems, and Pi is perfect for tinkering because it is minimal and can be ripped apart and reassembled.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to Pi and OpenClaw
sections.summary: Luebken introduces his exploration of Pi through OpenClaw, noting he is building agents at Seven AI. He references Mario's morning talk about a minimal coding agent and encourages the audience to experiment. He notes Mario is joining Arendelle.

sections.title: The philosophy of coding agents (doing one thing well)
sections.summary: Cites Ken Thompson's Unix principle of programs doing one thing well as aligning with agents. Uses Cohere/Claude desktop as example: Excel support comes from bundling small CLI tools (Pandas, OpenPyXL, LibreOffice), not direct Excel integration. Notes no authoritative patterns exist yet.

sections.title: Architectural pattern: Making systems easy for agents
sections.summary: Introduces the key architectural pattern: make systems easy for coding agents. Don't add complexity; think about what the agent is good at and design accordingly. Sets up the agenda for the talk.

sections.title: Defining an agent: LLM with tools in a loop
sections.summary: Defines an agent as an LLM running tools in a loop with goals and context. Shows Pi's TypeScript agent class, event system, and hooks for pre-tool-call logic such as authorization and role-based access control.

sections.title: Practical example: CRM lead qualifier
sections.summary: Demonstrates a CRM lead qualifier with terminal interface using about three TypeScript files. Shows tool calls, results, scoring leads, system prompts, hooks for authorization, and event subscriptions for tool call results.

sections.title: Coding agents vs. core agents
sections.summary: Explains coding agents are the same as core agents but with a runtime and shell (Bash). Shares Peter's OpenClaw example: a voice message was handled by the agent discovering and using FFmpeg, appearing to learn but actually just calling available tools.

sections.title: Extension API and UI interactions
sections.summary: Covers Pi's extension API focusing on session events and UI interaction. Shows a new pipeline command with context UI select enabling front-end interaction. Notes Pi built a web UI using the same extension mechanism. Current extensions are tailored to coding agents; refactoring underway for broader use.

sections.title: Multi-channel environment: Pi and OpenClaw
sections.summary: Introduces Pi and OpenClaw as a multi-channel environment. Lists Pi's packages: coding agent, agent core, Pi AI (unified LLM abstraction), and terminal UI interface. OpenClaw has its own plugin mechanism for multi-channel routing, provider orchestration, sub-agents, and gateway support, built around Pi's core mechanics.

sections.title: Real-world B2B sales pipeline application
sections.summary: Describes a client application for a B2B sales process. Incoming RFP emails are monitored and routed through a gateway to customer-specific agents. Each agent has a general harness file (Agent MDE) defining its role and a customer-specific file (Customer MD) for quirks, discounts, and access. Sessions are created and reused per case. CRM and ERP data is exposed via CLIs in a sandbox. Mentions exploring Nvidia's open shell for sandboxing.

sections.title: Demonstration: Dashboard and email drafting process
sections.summary: Shows the dashboard with an email inbox. An RFP email is identified by an LLM call, associated with a case and agent session, and a draft email is generated. The user stays in their inbox and can freely edit the draft. Behind the scenes, multiple agents work with tool calls in loops to produce the output.

sections.title: Final takeaways and encouragement to tinker
sections.summary: Luebken closes with key takeaways: coding agents are and will be a core building block for software systems, many people are betting on it. Pi is minimal and perfect for tinkering—rip it apart and put it together. Encourages the audience to give it a try.
